title: Competition and moral behavior: A meta-analysis of forty-five crowd-sourced experimental designs

source.title: Competition and moral behavior: A meta-analysis of forty-five crowd-sourced experimental designs
source.authors: Christoph Huber; Anna Dreber; Jürgen Huber; Magnus Johannesson; Michael Kirchler; Utz Weitzel; and collaborating authors (full list in cited article)

evidence.quote: Does competition affect moral behavior? This fundamental question has been debated for centuries
In a large-scale online data collection, 18,123 experimental participants were randomly allocated to 45 randomly selected experimental designs out of 95 submitted designs.
We find a small adverse effect of competition on moral behavior in a meta-analysis of the pooled data.
We find substantial design heterogeneity—estimated to be about 1.6 times as large as the average standard error of effect size estimates of the 45 research designs
We invited research teams (RTs) to independently design and implement an online experiment with one competition and one control condition.
but they were required to use an “experimental economics protocol” with monetary incentives and no deception (20).

Participants in the experiments were randomly assigned to one of the 45 × 2 experimental treatments, and 18,123 completed observations (about 400 per design) were collected via Prolific in January 2022.
The average age of the Prolific participants who completed the experiment was 32.5 y (sd = 12.3), and 55.5% were female.
Of the participants, 32.5% were from the United Kingdom, 15.1% from the United States, and 11.7% from South Africa.
The average Prolific approval rate of the participants was 99.5 (sd = 1.0), and English is the first language for 48.1% of the sample.
Of the participants, 34.4% are fully employed, and 39.2% are students.

102 RTs were invited to submit a research design, 95 RTs submitted a research design, of which 50 RTs were randomly selected to participate in the study, and of which, 45 RTs delivered the experimental software and were thus included in the data collection.
Our hypotheses and tests follow a detailed preanalysis plan (PAP) registered prior to starting the data collection (osf.io/r6anc).
As preregistered, we use the threshold of P < 0.005 for “statistically significant evidence” and P < 0.05 for “suggestive evidence” (23).
Our first primary hypothesis is that competition affects moral behavior.
This hypothesis is not directional, as different scholars have argued for both a negative and a positive effect of competition on moral behavior
The meta-analytic effect size in Cohen’s d units is −0.085 (95% CI [−0.147, −0.022], P = 0.008) for analytic approach A and −0.086 (95% CI [−0.144, −0.027], P = 0.004) for analytic approach B.
Our second primary hypothesis is that effect size estimates vary across research designs over and above the variation expected from pure sampling variation (i.e., the within-study variance).
Based on Cochran’s Q tests, we find statistically significant heterogeneity for both analytic approach A (Q(44) = 181.1, P < 0.001) and analytic approach B (Q(44) = 161.5, P < 0.001).

According to the estimated I2 for analytic approach B, 72.8% (95% CI [64.8, 85.8]) of the variation in results across research designs is attributable to design heterogeneity; the corresponding result for analytic approach A is 75.7% (95% CI [66.2, 86.0]).

Our first secondary hypothesis is that the effect sizes vary systematically with the average quality ratings.
In secondary hypothesis 2, we test whether there is heterogeneity in the estimated effect sizes across research designs after controlling for the rated quality.

an experimental design—which is not incorporated into standard

illustrating that a single design is largely uninformative about
whether or not the underlying hypothesis is supported. The aver-

Participating RTs were required to design (and later program) an experiment with one competition and one control treatment to be administered online via Prolific with a total sample size of n = 400 participants for each design/experiment.
Designs had to be implemented in a between-subjects setting (with, in expectation, equally sized control and treatment groups of n = 200 each).
The fixed payment (show-up fee) will be £1.30 for all experiments.
a) fluency in English and b) approval rate above 90%.
It is not allowed to exclude (screen out) any of the randomly assigned subjects from participating in the experiment.
At the common welcome screen, all participants were required to sign a capt-
cha (to rule out bots), to provide informed consent, and to complete a common attention check question (see Addendum Appendix 1 in the addendum to the PAP for these screens; osf.io/r6anc).

After that, participants were randomly redirected to the 90 (45 designs × 2 treatments) individual treatments in batches of four participants, i.e., four participants in a row were redirected to the same treatment of the same experiment/design.
We collected the data in ten time slots during the 2 wk from January 17 to January 28, 2022
In the end, we reached 18,123 completed observations.

RTs were asked to assess each other’s designs anonymously (based on the preregistration template submitted by each RT). In particular, each RT was asked to assess ten other randomly selected designs and rate them on a Likert scale from 0 to 10
We demean the RTs’ quality ratings (i.e., we subtract the mean rating of an RT from every rating of this RT) before we estimate the average peer assessment score for each design.
We tried to rule out repeated participation, but 709 participants still managed to participate in the study again.

Standardizing effect sizes across RTs: For each RT study, we estimate the effect size and standard error according to the proposed/preregistered analysis and econometric specification that has been preferred by the RT as the best approach to answer the research question

To remove as much of the analytical variation across RTs as possible, we estimate the meta-analytic effect size and between-study heterogeneity based on a standardized analytical approach across the RT designs.
The data and analysis code are available at the project’s OSF repository (osf.io/r6anc).

The 45 RTs consisted of 86 researchers, of which 17.4% did not hold a PhD, 43.0% held a PhD in economics, 26.7% held a PhD in psychology, 5.8% held a PhD in behavioral sciences, 4.7% held a PhD in business studies, and 2.3% held a PhD in finance.
We decided to include at most 50 research designs and as we received 95 designs, we randomly selected 50 designs out of those for inclusion in the study.
Assuming an independent-samples t test, with n1 = n2 = 200, gives us 90% power to detect an effect size of d = 0.411 and d = 0.324 at the 0.5% and the 5% significance thresholds.

strong evidence for systematic variation in meta-analytic effects
attributable to these three design characteristics. However, it
should be noted that the statistical power is limited for detecting
differences between subgroups of designs.

studies.title: Crowd-sourced online experiment: 45 designs, competition versus control
studies.description: 18,123 Prolific participants randomly allocated, in batches of four, to the competition or control treatment of 45 independently designed experiments.

studies.title: Peer assessment of the designs by the research teams
studies.description: Before data collection each research team rated ten other designs on a 0 to 10 informativeness scale.

studies.title: Prospective meta-analysis of the 45 design effects
studies.description: Random-effects meta-analysis of the 45 design-level Cohen's d estimates, heterogeneity, moderator and robustness analyses.

fields.label: Method type
fields.value: Crowd-sourced many-designs online experiment with a prospective random-effects meta-analysis

fields.label: Summary
fields.value: 45 independent research teams each contributed an online experiment with one competition and one control condition on the question whether competition affects moral behavior; 18,123 Prolific participants were randomly allocated across the 90 treatments and the 45 effect sizes were meta-analysed.

fields.label: Question
fields.value: Does competition affect moral behavior?

fields.label: Gap
fields.value: Existing experimental studies rely on single, idiosyncratic designs and give inconclusive evidence; variation in true effect sizes across reasonable designs (design heterogeneity) is not part of common inference.

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Competition affects moral behavior (non-directional).

fields.label: Scope
fields.value: Primary hypothesis 1, tested in analytic approaches A and B

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Effect size estimates vary across research designs over and above sampling variation (design heterogeneity).

fields.label: Scope
fields.value: Primary hypothesis 2

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Effect sizes vary systematically with the average peer quality ratings.

fields.label: Scope
fields.value: Secondary hypothesis 1

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: There is heterogeneity in effect sizes across designs after controlling for rated quality.

fields.label: Scope
fields.value: Secondary hypothesis 2

fields.label: Definition
fields.value: Moral behavior is measured without competition, in each research team's own design.

fields.label: Definition
fields.value: Moral behavior is measured under competition, operationalized differently by each research team.

fields.label: Setting
fields.value: Online, via Prolific, in ten time slots between 17 and 28 January 2022

fields.label: Recruitment
fields.value: One common Prolific study; participants invited from Prolific users who are fluent in English with an approval rate above 90%

fields.label: Eligibility
fields.value: Fluency in English and approval rate above 90%; randomly assigned subjects could not be screened out

fields.label: Unit of analysis
fields.value: Participant (one observation per participant; batches of four were the unit of randomization)

fields.label: Compensation
fields.value: Fixed payment (show-up fee) of £1.30 for all experiments plus design-specific bonus payments

fields.label: Attrition
fields.value: Average attrition 7.9% in the competition and 8.6% in the control treatment

fields.label: Repeated participation
fields.value: 709 participants participated again; all their subsequent observations were excluded

fields.label: Type
fields.value: Between-subjects; each of 45 designs has one competition and one control treatment, with a target n of 400 per design

fields.label: Assignment
fields.value: Participants were randomly redirected to the 90 treatments in batches of four

fields.label: Selection of designs
fields.value: 50 of 95 submitted designs were drawn at random; 45 teams delivered software and were implemented

fields.label: Design requirements
fields.value: No deception at any time, monetary incentives, between-subjects variation, instructions in English

fields.label: Answer
fields.value: A small adverse effect of competition on moral behavior (d about −0.085) and substantial design heterogeneity (tau about 1.6 times the average standard error), so single designs are of limited informativeness and generalizability.

fields.label: Limitations
fields.value: Only designs implementable online; English-speaking Prolific participants who compete with strangers; results may differ in the lab or field.
